title: Depend on abstractions
idea: The Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP) says business policy must not depend on concrete details; both depend on an abstraction the policy owns.

analogy.text: A laptop declares the charging port it needs. Any charger built to that port works, and the laptop never changes for a new charger brand.
analogy.breaks: Ports are industry standards; your interfaces are written by the policy code.

points: High-level code holds business rules; low-level code talks to mail, databases and files.
The policy declares an interface in its own terms; details implement it.
Only one place, the composition root, calls `new` on concrete details and wires them.
DIP is the design rule; dependency injection (DI) is the technique that delivers it.

hero.title: Wiring once, calling through the port

messages.label: new EmailNotifier(host)
messages.note: Only the composition root names the concrete class and knows its config.

messages.label: new InvoiceService(notifier)
messages.note: The service receives the detail through its constructor. It never builds one itself.

messages.label: invoiceIssued(invoice)
messages.note: In source code the service calls only `InvoiceNotifier`, an interface it owns.

messages.label: dispatch at runtime
messages.note: At runtime the call lands on whichever implementation main passed in.

messages.label: returns
messages.note: The detail does its work and returns. The service never learns the transport.

messages.label: new InvoiceService(fake)
messages.note: A test wires a recording fake instead. The policy code stays untouched.

code.title: The problem
code.caption: `InvoiceService` builds its own `SmtpMailer`. A plain unit test now emails a real customer.

walk.text: `SmtpMailer` is a low-level detail. A static counter stands in for real side effects.
The policy calls `new SmtpMailer` in a field. The arrow points from rules down to transport.
The business rule validates and numbers invoices, then is welded to SMTP.
A unit test only wants to check the invoice id. It cannot swap the mailer out.
The output shows the cost: the test opened a connection and sent mail.

code.title: The fix
code.caption: The service owns `InvoiceNotifier`; email and a test fake both implement it. Wiring lives in `main`.

walk.text: `Invoice` is an immutable record that rejects bad input at construction.
The port is named for what the policy needs: news that an invoice exists.
`InvoiceService` takes the port by constructor and rejects null. It imports no SMTP code.
`EmailNotifier` depends on the abstraction. Its host config stays with the detail.
`RecordingNotifier` is a test fake. It returns a copy of what it saw.
`main` is the composition root: production and test wire different details into the same policy.

pitfalls: Naming the interface after the detail, like `SmtpGateway`, still leaks the transport into the policy.
Adding an interface for every class with one implementation and no test seam is overkill.
Calling `new` on details inside services, or a static `getInstance()`, silently undoes the inversion.

quiz.q: Ops wants invoices sent by SMS instead of email. With the fix, what changes?
options: A new `SmsNotifier` class, and one line in `main`
`EmailNotifier` is edited to also send SMS
quiz.why: The policy depends only on `InvoiceNotifier`. A new detail implements it, and the composition root passes it in. Policy and port stay unchanged.

takeaway: Policy owns the interface; details plug in from the edge.

starters: What is the difference between DIP and dependency injection?
